title: The power plants inside your cells were once free-living bacteria
body: Mitochondria, which make ATP, the chemical fuel used throughout the cell, are thought to descend from bacteria that another single-celled organism took in but never digested. The guests lived on inside, and their descendants became a permanent part of the cell. When it happened is unresolved, though fossils of complex cells suggest it was more than 1.6 billion years ago. The idea, called symbiogenesis or endosymbiotic theory, was championed by Lynn Margulis in 1967 and is now the leading explanation for the origin of complex cells; plant chloroplasts are thought to come from captured cyanobacteria in the same way.

slides.alt: Animation of a pastel cell interior with glowing membranes: a host cell wraps its membrane around a bacterium, which lives on inside, divides and becomes mitochondria. A bacterium and a mitochondrion then sit side by side, showing circular DNA, two membranes, splitting in two and ribosomes.

slides.prompt: Run the four tests on a bacterium, a mitochondrion and the cell’s own nucleus and ribosomes. Which two keep matching?
slides.takeaway: Circular DNA, splitting in two, cardiolipin, ribosomes jammed by an antibiotic for bacteria: each time the mitochondrion matches the bacterium, not the cell it lives in.

slides.heading: How a cell got its power plants

steps.label: A single-celled host engulfs a bacterium
The bacterium survives and lives inside it
Over a billion years on: your mitochondria

slides.heading: When did it happen?
slides.text: Nobody knows exactly. The oldest fossils that are surely complex cells are about 1.6 billion years old, so the bacteria must have moved in before then. Estimates from molecular clocks vary widely.

slides.heading: Not a new idea
slides.text: The Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski set out the theory in 1905 and 1910. Lynn Margulis took it up in 1967 and backed it with microbiological evidence, in a paper called “On the origin of mitosing cells”.

slides.question: In the same theory, where do plant chloroplasts come from?
slides.explanation: Endosymbiotic theory holds that chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria taken in by another cell, just as mitochondria descend from engulfed bacteria.

slides.heading: Match each feature to its bacterial echo
slides.explanation: Circular DNA, division like binary fission, cardiolipin and porins are all bacterial traits, the fingerprints of the mitochondrion’s ancestry.
